name: trim_decision_ctt
prompt: I have eval results for several versions of my agent skill across ~22 cases (evals/fixtures/results_5versions.csv: columns taker_id,item_id,score,seed). I want to shrink this suite without losing signal. Which cases should I cut, which are dead weight, and which must I keep? Tell me what's actually going on with each.
response:
Here's the full picture.

---

## Regime & setup

10 takers (opus, sonnet, haiku, v5–v1, noskill, ablation_norefs) × 22 cases × 3 seeds = small-N iteration regime. No free IRT. CTT + G-theory is the right stack here, and with 10 takers the bootstrapped CIs are wide enough that you need to be careful about trimming on a point estimate alone.

Labels look programmatic (0/1), so no judge gate needed.

---

## Reliability verdict first

**Eρ² = 0.912 [0.815, 0.942]** — dependable enough to rank versions. Φ = 0.878 — dependable for threshold decisions too. The suite is not the problem. The D-study shows 11 items gets you to Eρ² ≈ 0.84, so you have a lot of room to trim before reliability degrades below 0.80.

One flag worth noting upfront: **seed/run variance (0.142) is larger than your version×item residual (0.082).** Adding seeds buys more precision than adding cases. If 3 seeds per cell is your current design, bumping to 5 would tighten your version rankings more than expanding the case pool.

---

## What to do with each case

### URGENT FIX — do not trim

**`case_inverted`** (p=0.40, r_rest=−0.846, D=−0.778; CI: [−0.992, −0.539])

This is your only broken item, and the CI makes it unambiguous — the full interval is firmly negative. The best-performing takers (opus, sonnet, higher-tier versions) are *failing* this case more than the weaker ones. That's almost certainly an inverted gold label or an inverted rubric check, not a nuanced case. **Fix the gold label before your next eval run.** Once corrected, this becomes your highest-discriminating item — r_rest magnitude of 0.846 puts it in the top tier of the suite. Don't cut it, fix it.

---

### TRIM — dead weight

**`case_saturated`** (p=1.000, r=NaN, D=0.000)

Every taker passes on every seed. Zero discrimination by construction — it cannot contribute to any version comparison. Cut it unless it's explicitly guarding a regression you care about, in which case label it `guard` and keep it. Ask yourself: "Was there ever a version that failed this?" If not, trim.

**`case_09`** (p=0.267, r_rest=0.133; CI: [−0.728, 0.847])

The point estimate looks neutral-to-low, but the CI tells the real story: this case is statistically unknown. It spans from "strongly negative" to "informative" with equal plausibility at 10 takers. You simply don't have the data to trust this item in either direction. Trim it — or if it covers a unique capability nothing else tests, hold it and add more takers before deciding.

---

### TRIM ONE — perfect duplicate

**`case_00` ↔ `case_dupe00`** (pairwise r = 1.0 across takers)

These two cases produce identical pass/fail patterns for every taker on every seed. They're testing the exact same thing. Keep whichever has better provenance or a more clearly specified rubric; trim the other. This gives you the biggest free reliability-per-item gain after the fixes above.

---

### KEEP — the discriminating core

These 10 items have both mid-range difficulty and discrimination CI comfortably above zero:

| Case | p | r_rest | CI lower | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| case_07 | 0.53 | 0.885 | 0.768 | Best discriminator in suite |
| case_06 | 0.80 | 0.888 | 0.817 | Best discriminator, slightly easy |
| case_13 | 0.70 | 0.898 | 0.704 | Near-ceiling but still separating |
| case_12 | 0.67 | 0.868 | 0.713 | Solid mid-range |
| case_11 | 0.47 | 0.833 | 0.632 | Core signal item |
| case_17 | 0.77 | 0.781 | 0.272 | Good point, CI acceptable |
| case_15 | 0.60 | 0.669 | 0.299 | Mid-range, well targeted |
| case_08 | 0.50 | 0.659 | 0.363 | Clean mid-range |
| case_02 | 0.43 | 0.655 | 0.147 | |
| case_01 | 0.60 | 0.718 | 0.237 | |

---

### KEEP — wider CIs but no evidence to cut

These items have positive point estimates but wide enough CIs that you shouldn't cut on uncertainty alone:

| Case | p | r_rest | CI | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| case_04 | 0.73 | 0.739 | [0.154, 0.929] | Positive but wide lower bound |
| case_05 | 0.73 | 0.660 | [0.314, 0.963] | Similar |
| case_03 | 0.50 | 0.432 | [−0.110, 0.806] | Low lower bound; keep if unique capability |
| case_14 | 0.80 | 0.385 | [−0.634, 0.843] | Very wide — only keep if it covers something unique |
| case_16 | 0.77 | 0.509 | [−0.289, 0.911] | Same |
| case_noise | 0.43 | 0.407 | [−0.508, 0.944] | Very wide — check if this is a synthetic noise case |
| case_10 | 0.23 | 0.655 | [0.246, 0.930] | Floored but CI clearly positive; hard, not broken |

`case_10` is floored (p=0.23) but discriminates — it's genuinely hard for these takers, not broken. Keep as a ceiling-break item for your stronger variants.

---

## Recommended trimmed suite

Cut `case_saturated`, `case_09`, and one of `case_00`/`case_dupe00` (−3 cases). Fix `case_inverted`. That leaves **19 items** with projected Eρ² ≈ 0.90 — well above the 0.80 decision threshold, and you've eliminated all the noise-generators without losing any signal.

If you want to trim more aggressively to ~12–13 items, the items with lower-bound CIs dipping negative (`case_03`, `case_14`, `case_16`, `case_noise`) are the next candidates — but only after verifying no unique capability is lost, and only once you bump seeds to 5 to compensate for the reduced n.

assertions.text: Reports per-item difficulty AND discrimination, not just a mean pass rate
Flags the negative-discrimination item (case_inverted) as a FIX / broken item rather than a trim
Recommends trimming the saturated and/or non-discriminating items
Raises the guard-item exception (saturated items guarding a known regression should be kept)
Acknowledges small-N uncertainty (intervals / caution) rather than acting on point estimates
